title: Sliding window: best sum of k in a row
content:
def max_sum_k(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]  # add new, drop old
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

print(max_sum_k([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3))  # 9
why_it_matters: Reusing the last window's sum makes it O(n) instead of O(n * k).

title: Binary search, the safe way
why_it_matters: lo + (hi - lo) // 2 avoids integer overflow in Java and C++, a classic interview follow-up.

title: bisect finds the insert position
content:
import bisect

scores = [10, 20, 30, 40]
pos = bisect.bisect_left(scores, 25)
print(pos)  # 2, where 25 would go

bisect.insort(scores, 25)  # insert and keep it sorted
print(scores)  # [10, 20, 25, 30, 40]
why_it_matters: Python's bisect gives you a tested binary search in one line.

title: Two pointers: is it a palindrome?
why_it_matters: Two pointers moving inward check the whole string in one O(n) pass.

title: Prefix sums for fast range totals
content:
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
prefix = [0]
for n in nums:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + n)

# sum of nums[i..j] = prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i]
print(prefix[4] - prefix[1])  # 1 + 4 + 1 = 6
why_it_matters: After one O(n) pass, every range sum is O(1). Many subarray problems start here.

title: Top k with heapq
content:
import heapq

nums = [5, 1, 9, 3, 7]
print(heapq.nlargest(2, nums))   # [9, 7]
print(heapq.nsmallest(2, nums))  # [1, 3]

heap = []
for n in nums:
    heapq.heappush(heap, -n)  # negate for a max-heap
print(-heap[0])  # 9
why_it_matters: heapq is a min-heap only. Push negative numbers when you need a max-heap.

why_it_matters: Counter counts items in O(n) and makes frequency problems one-liners.

why_it_matters: Caching results turns exponential recursion into O(n). This is top-down DP.

title: Union-Find with path compression
why_it_matters: Union-Find answers 'are these connected?' almost in O(1). Used in Kruskal and cycle checks.

title: Bit tricks: power of two
content:
def is_power_of_two(n):
    # a power of two has exactly one 1 bit
    return n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0

print(is_power_of_two(16))  # True
print(is_power_of_two(18))  # False
print(bin(18).count("1"))   # 2 set bits
why_it_matters: n & (n - 1) removes the lowest 1 bit. It shows up in many bit problems.

title: Python sorts with Timsort
content: Python's sort() and sorted() use Timsort, written by Tim Peters in 2002. It mixes merge sort and insertion sort, and is very fast on data that is already partly sorted.
why_it_matters: Python's sort is O(n log n) and stable, so equal items keep their order.

title: Dijkstra's 20-minute algorithm
content: Edsger Dijkstra designed his shortest-path algorithm in about 20 minutes in 1956, while sitting at a cafe in Amsterdam, without pen and paper. He published it in 1959.
why_it_matters: It still powers route finding in maps and network routing today.

title: The binary search bug in Java
content: In 2006 Joshua Bloch wrote that Java's own binary search had a bug for years: (low + high) / 2 can overflow when the array is huge. The fix is low + (high - low) / 2.
why_it_matters: Even simple code has edge cases. Interviewers love to ask about this one.

title: Quicksort was born in Moscow
content: Tony Hoare invented quicksort in 1959 while he was a visiting student in Moscow. He needed to sort words for a Russian to English translation program.
why_it_matters: Quicksort's partition idea is behind Quickselect, which finds the k-th smallest item.

title: Merge sort is from 1945
content: John von Neumann invented merge sort in 1945, one of the earliest sorting algorithms written for a computer.
why_it_matters: Merge sort is the classic example of divide and conquer, and it is stable.

title: The first hash table idea
content: Hans Peter Luhn at IBM wrote about hashing in 1953, including putting items that clash into chained lists.
why_it_matters: Python's dict and set are hash tables, which is why lookups are O(1) on average.

title: Graph theory began with seven bridges
content: In 1736 Leonhard Euler proved you cannot walk across all seven bridges of Konigsberg exactly once. This is seen as the start of graph theory.
why_it_matters: Every graph problem you solve today goes back to this puzzle.

title: Why it is called dynamic programming
content: Richard Bellman named dynamic programming in the 1950s. He wrote that he picked the name partly because it sounded impressive and hid that he was doing mathematical research.
why_it_matters: The name says little. The idea is simple: solve small subproblems once and reuse them.

title: Trie comes from retrieval
content: Edward Fredkin coined the name trie in 1960, from the word retrieval. He said it like tree, but many people say try to tell it apart.
why_it_matters: Tries power autocomplete and prefix search.

title: The tortoise and the hare
content: Floyd's cycle detection uses a slow pointer and a fast pointer. If there is a loop, the fast one catches up with the slow one. It needs only O(1) extra memory.
why_it_matters: This is the standard answer for Linked List Cycle and Find the Duplicate Number.

title: A* was built for a robot
content: The A* search algorithm was published in 1968 by Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson and Bertram Raphael at SRI, for the Shakey robot project.
why_it_matters: A* adds a smart guess (heuristic) to Dijkstra, and is used in games and maps.

title: Python dicts keep insertion order
content: Since Python 3.7, dict keeps keys in the order you inserted them. This is part of the language, not just a detail of one version.
why_it_matters: You can build an ordered result straight from a dict without sorting again.

title: Python ints never overflow
content: Python's int has arbitrary precision, so it grows as big as memory allows. Java's int stops at 2^31 - 1 and wraps around.
why_it_matters: Overflow bugs from Java or C++ will not show in Python, but interviewers may still ask about them.

title: KMP string search
content: The Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm was published in 1977. It finds a pattern in text in O(n + m) by never moving backward in the text.
why_it_matters: Its prefix table idea is used in many string problems.

title: Bloom filters say maybe
content: Burton Bloom described the Bloom filter in 1970. It can say an item is definitely not in a set, or probably is, using very little memory.
why_it_matters: Databases and browsers use them to skip slow lookups.
